facts.claim: "Headphones On" was released April 18, 2025 on Columbia Records as the fourth single from Addison Rae's debut studio album Addison.
Rae co-wrote the song with its producers, Luka Kloser and Elvira Anderfjärd.
It was the first release under Rae's new publishing deal with Sony Music Publishing.
Rae recorded the song in Stockholm while she was sick. The credited studio is MXM.
Rae described the song as one of her most emotional to date and as cathartic to make.
The music video was directed by Mitch Ryan and filmed in Reykjavík, Iceland. It shows Rae daydreaming during grocery shopping and imagining herself in the Icelandic countryside.
Slant described the track as having a new jack swing bounce, while Stardust Magazine said it blends trip-hop and early-2000s pop influences, citing Britney Spears, Madonna and Björk.
The lyrics deal with her parents' publicized 2022 divorce, the pressures of fame, and escapism.
The song became Rae's second Billboard Hot 100 entry after "Diet Pepsi" and her second top-40 hit in the UK and Ireland.
Rae's first major-label single, "Diet Pepsi", came out on Columbia Records in 2024. The album Addison was produced by Anderfjärd and Kloser, who co-wrote its songs with her.

research.lineage: It sits in the 2020s pop revival of 1990s and early-2000s sounds, with new jack swing and trip-hop touches, and is a confessional closer on the debut album of a former TikTok star turned pop singer.

draft:
The saddest line in **Headphones On** comes with a shrug: "Wish my mom and dad could've been in love." Addison Rae doesn't dress it up. The next line just accepts it, guessing some things weren't meant to last, and moves on to comparing herself to "the new it girl." The song is about her parents' publicized 2022 divorce, the pressure of fame, and the urge to get away from both. It handles all of it the way a lot of people handle a bad week: put the music on, turn it up, and keep going.

That's the emotional trick here. The chorus is an escape plan, and the verses keep showing what she's escaping from. Pain, a cigarette to feel better, and then the small, stubborn detail that gives the song its spine: "So I still get dolled up." It isn't denial. It's dignity held in place with eyeliner. Hurt and vanity sit next to each other without canceling out, and the song doesn't ask you to pick one. Even the bridge's life lesson, that you can't fix what's already broken and have to surrender to the moment, sounds less like wisdom than something she keeps repeating until it sticks.

Rae wrote it with her producers, Luka Kloser and Elvira Anderfjärd, the pair behind the whole album, and recorded it in Stockholm at MXM while she was sick. She has called it one of her most emotional songs and said making it was cathartic. The arrangement doesn't pour that out. Sustained synth-pad chords hang in the background while kick, snare, and hi-hat hold a steady, moderate beat. A bass synth loops a simple line, and a separate synth melody weaves around the vocal. The production is polished and clean, with a little reverb opening up the voice. Rae sings smoothly and clearly, stacked with harmonies in thirds, never pushing.

Slant heard new jack swing bounce in it. Stardust Magazine pointed to trip-hop and early-2000s pop, naming Britney Spears, Madonna, and Björk. Both make sense. This is the 2020s revival of turn-of-the-millennium pop, but bent toward confession rather than the dance floor. The coda gives the game away. It keeps chanting "Cut the tears, cut the tears 'til the wheels fall off," a mantra for shutting feeling down that gets more insistent the longer it runs.

It sticks because it captures something everyone has done: hurting, putting on your favorite song, and letting a cool, steady beat carry you through a feeling you're not ready to look at yet.
